impact_families.title: Spanish nutrient statement requires identical lettering
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualifying claim uses an equally prominent nutrient statement in a different typeface and requires a lettering change.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns presentation of a required statement. It does not alter nutrient thresholds or the substantive category covered by the derogation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Identical lettering may be interpreted as a functional prominence requirement.

impact_families.title: French high-unsaturated-fat thresholds leave the denominator unclear
impact_families.effect: A food satisfies the fatty-acid-share and energy tests but cannot bear the relevant claim because its whole-product percentage falls below the French threshold reading.
impact_families.rationale: The denominator directly changes eligibility for three nutrition claims whose Annex conditions are binding through Article 8.
impact_families.uncertainty: The nutritional context and otherwise partly redundant energy tests strongly support a total-fatty-acid denominator.

impact_families.title: Croatian evaluation duty refers broadly to other diseases
impact_families.effect: The evaluation addresses a relevant communicable disease as part of its coverage of other diseases.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns the scope of an evaluation report and does not itself alter food-claim eligibility, sanctions or remedies.
impact_families.uncertainty: The dietary context may narrow the diseases relevant to the report.

impact_families.title: Maltese high-unsaturated-fat condition omits the minimum qualifier
impact_families.effect: A product with 80% unsaturated fatty acids and over 20% of energy from unsaturated fat could fail an exact-70% reading.
impact_families.rationale: If exactness prevailed, the claim would be unavailable throughout the otherwise qualifying range above 70%, materially narrowing its substantive eligibility.
impact_families.uncertainty: The claim's purpose and neighbouring minimum thresholds strongly favour harmonisation.

impact_families.title: Italian association exception is not expressly limited to health-related bodies
impact_families.effect: A health claim refers to a recommendation by a voluntary association unrelated to health and falls outside Article 12(c)’s prohibition under the Italian reading.
impact_families.rationale: Article 12(c)’s express cross-reference makes the association category determine the reach of an outright prohibition, while other claim requirements remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The health-claim context may restrict voluntary associations to health-related bodies.

impact_families.title: Italian nutrient-profile disclosure has weaker placement requirements
impact_families.effect: The prescribed nutrient disclosure appears on the same packaging side as the claim but farther away and in smaller print.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change concerns presentation within an existing exception. Disclosure, the single-nutrient limit and other claim requirements remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: General anti-misleading rules may constrain inconspicuous presentation but do not expressly restore the omitted requirements.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian narrows the express weight-control category to weight loss
impact_families.effect: A weight-maintenance claim outside Article 13's other categories could be excluded from its list-based permission under the Lithuanian reading.
impact_families.rationale: The difference could change eligibility for an express route permitting health claims, subject to scientific substantiation and inclusion in the authorised list.
impact_families.uncertainty: The bodily-function category or contextual interpretation could cover particular weight-maintenance claims.

impact_families.title: Maltese permits alternative channels for additional authorisation warnings
impact_families.effect: An opinion and draft authorisation could specify an additional statement in only one channel, while the independent Article 10 duties remain applicable.
impact_families.rationale: The established change concerns channel coverage of additional particulars. The supplied text does not identify a particular omitted warning or establish removal of a core health-protection duty.
impact_families.uncertainty: The final authorisation could require both channels; the additional statement's content is unspecified.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian assessment period starts at submission rather than receipt
impact_families.effect: Where submission precedes receipt by the Authority, the Lithuanian wording could require an earlier opinion.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns the assessment timetable. Article 18 does not make expiry itself authorise a claim or determine substantive eligibility.
impact_families.uncertainty: The relevant submission stage is unspecified, and submission and receipt may coincide.

impact_families.title: Latvian transitional stock rule uses entry into force as its cutoff
impact_families.effect: Non-compliant stock labelled after entry into force but before application could lose continued-sale permission under Article 28(1), unless another transition protects it.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes eligibility for an express permission to market otherwise non-compliant stock until expiry, subject to the July 2009 ceiling.
impact_families.uncertainty: The publication date and actual stock are not established; other specific transitions may apply.

impact_families.title: Maltese replaces the trans-fat no-increase safeguard with saturated fat
impact_families.effect: A product sufficiently reduces saturated fat and the combined fatty-acid total but increases trans fat; the Maltese safeguard could allow the claim that English excludes.
impact_families.rationale: The substitution removes the express trans-fat no-increase condition, independently changing substantive eligibility for the claim.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation could restore the trans-fat reference.

impact_families.title: Latvian saturated-fat-free test omits trans-fatty acids
impact_families.effect: A food below the saturated-fat limit but above the combined saturated-fat and trans-fatty-acid limit could satisfy the Latvian numerical condition.
impact_families.rationale: The omission removes an entire constituent from a substantive eligibility condition for a regulated absence claim.
impact_families.uncertainty: General safeguards remain, and contextual interpretation could restore the combined limit.

impact_families.title: Danish high-unsaturated-fat claims include exactly 20% energy
impact_families.effect: A product deriving exactly 20% of its energy from the relevant fat and meeting all other conditions qualifies for the corresponding Danish claim.
impact_families.rationale: The change is confined to equality at one numerical boundary for three nutrition descriptors. It does not change permission to market the food or other claim requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: Measurement and rounding rules are not supplied.

impact_families.title: Maltese register requirement points to a nonexistent paragraph
impact_families.effect: Measures adopted under Article 23(3) could be omitted from the public register if the Maltese cross-reference is applied without correction.
impact_families.rationale: The identified effect concerns register completeness and public information, without altering the measures' substantive requirements or adoption conditions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The adjacent provisions strongly support correcting the reference to Article 23(3).

impact_families.title: Finnish transitional deadline includes 19 January 2008
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualifying application made on 19 January preserves continued use of a health claim under Finnish but misses the literal English deadline.
impact_families.rationale: The date determines eligibility for an express transitional permission, rather than merely the timing of administrative processing.
impact_families.uncertainty: A harmonised interpretation of the deadline could eliminate the difference.

impact_families.title: Romanian omits relatedness from the commercial-name exemption
impact_families.effect: A name implying a health benefit could obtain the authorisation exemption through an accompanying compliant claim about an unrelated nutritional property.
impact_families.rationale: The omitted relationship materially broadens the possible scope of an express exemption from authorisation procedures.
impact_families.uncertainty: Relatedness may be inferred contextually; the general prohibition on misleading claims remains applicable.

impact_families.title: Greek no-added-sodium condition omits the ingredient's added-sodium qualifier
impact_families.effect: A food with no added salt and sodium below the ceiling loses claim eligibility because one ingredient naturally contains sodium.
impact_families.rationale: The unqualified ingredient exclusion can remove substantive permission to use the claim for a category of formulations otherwise satisfying the no-addition and numerical conditions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The heading and retained sodium ceiling strongly support an added-only interpretation.

impact_families.title: Maltese Article 18 scientific assessment deadline is four months
impact_families.effect: Without an extension, an opinion issued after four but within five months could comply with English while missing the Maltese deadline.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes an administrative assessment period. The supplied provisions attach no automatic authorisation, forfeiture or sanction to its expiry.
impact_families.uncertainty: No specific remedy for missing this deadline is established by the supplied text.

impact_families.title: Spanish implementation guidelines remain discretionary
impact_families.effect: Guidelines are considered appropriate but are not adopted, consistently with the Spanish discretionary formulation.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects an implementation-guidance duty, without directly changing authorisation criteria or entitlement to use a health claim.
impact_families.uncertainty: Discretion in determining appropriateness may substantially narrow the practical difference.

impact_families.title: Latvian low-saturated-fat energy test omits saturated fatty acids
impact_families.effect: A food meeting the mass condition could qualify despite saturated fatty acids providing over 10% of energy, if hydrogenated fatty acids alone remain within the energy ceiling.
impact_families.rationale: The omission removes saturated fatty acids from a substantive eligibility test for the low-saturated-fat claim.
impact_families.uncertainty: General scientific and non-misleading requirements remain; contextual interpretation could restore the combined test.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian notified-measures provision can read as a duty to implement
impact_families.effect: A Member State seeking to abandon notified legislation could instead be required to implement it after six months if the Commission's opinion is not negative.
impact_families.rationale: A mandatory reading would materially change the State's discretion whether to enact the proposed national measures.
impact_families.uncertainty: The notification framework supports interpreting the Lithuanian wording as permission.

impact_families.title: Greek reduced-nutrient exception names only trace elements
impact_families.effect: A vitamin-reduction claim meets the 10% reference-value exception but fails the general 30% reduction requirement and becomes impermissible under the Greek limitation.
impact_families.rationale: The narrower exception changes substantive claim eligibility for whole nutrient categories under Article 8, rather than merely adjusting presentation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The common Directive reference supports interpreting the exception as covering micronutrients generally.

impact_families.title: Romanian changes the trigger for the claimed-nutrient declaration rule
impact_families.effect: A voluntary claim could fall outside the specific Articles 31–34 declaration route while remaining subject to the following paragraph’s quantity-disclosure requirements.
impact_families.rationale: The residual difference concerns the governing declaration requirements. The incorporated provisions are absent, preventing a reliable assessment of their practical effect or magnitude.
impact_families.uncertainty: The definition of claims as non-mandatory and Article 7's surrounding text strongly favour a harmonised trigger.

impact_families.title: Slovak applies the unsaturated-fat threshold to a polyunsaturated-fat claim
impact_families.effect: A food satisfying the separate polyunsaturated-fat conditions but containing less than 70% total unsaturated fatty acids could lose permission to use the high-polyunsaturated-fat claim.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed sentence would add a materially different compositional threshold to Annex eligibility, which Article 8 makes a prerequisite for the claim.
impact_families.uncertainty: The matching heading and separate polyunsaturated entry strongly support interpreting the sentence as referring to unsaturated fat.

impact_families.title: Estonian Article 18 makes a protection request trigger restricted-use proceedings
impact_families.effect: Following an unfavourable opinion, a protection request requires the special route, imposing its five-year expiry on any authorisation subsequently granted.
impact_families.rationale: The trigger can determine the duration of permission, not merely administrative handling. Unrestricted continuation requires a further decision under point (b).
impact_families.uncertainty: The request does not establish scientific compliance, authorisation or satisfaction of Article 21.

impact_families.title: Estonian transitional notification names nutrition claims
impact_families.effect: A Member State supplies nutrition-claim information instead of the health-claim information identified by the preceding provision.
impact_families.rationale: The established difference concerns notification content. The surrounding health-claim procedure remains, and the text does not expressly make an individual claim’s eligibility depend on this notification.
impact_families.uncertainty: The health-claim antecedent and subsequent decision provision strongly support a harmonising reading.

impact_families.title: Maltese monounsaturated-fat percentage test counts unsaturated fat generally
impact_families.effect: A product meeting the monounsaturated energy requirement could qualify with at least 45% unsaturated fatty acids overall but less than 45% monounsaturated fatty acids.
impact_families.rationale: The broader nutrient category changes the substantive composition required for the high-monounsaturated-fat claim.
impact_families.uncertainty: The heading and monounsaturated energy condition support interpreting the percentage limb more narrowly.

impact_families.title: Latvian nutrient-profile exception names hydrogenated fatty acids
impact_families.effect: An otherwise compliant reduction claim concerning fatty acids within one category but outside the other could gain or lose exemption from the relevant nutrient profile.
impact_families.rationale: The substitution changes an express exception to a substantive condition for using nutrition claims.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context could treat the Latvian expression as intended to denote trans-fatty acids.

impact_families.title: Portuguese combines failures of health-claim prerequisites
impact_families.effect: If the combined-failure interpretation governed, a claim satisfying substantive requirements but lacking authorisation and listing could escape Article 10(1)'s express prohibition.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading weakens the central authorisation and listing gate for health claims. It does not establish that every such claim would escape other applicable restrictions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Articles 3, 5, 13 and 14 strongly support cumulative prerequisites.

impact_families.title: Finnish comparative claims require other manufacturers’ foods
impact_families.effect: A comparison using several brands from one manufacturer requires an additional comparator produced by another manufacturer.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence changes comparator selection while preserving the same-category, composition and range requirements. It does not independently expand or remove a class of authorised claims.
impact_families.uncertainty: A representative-range interpretation may already require external manufacturers under both versions.

impact_families.title: Maltese transitional application deadline can include 19 January 2008
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualifying health claim submitted for authorisation on 19 January 2008 could retain transitional permission under Maltese but fail the English date condition.
impact_families.rationale: The date controls continued permission to use the health claim during the authorisation process, rather than only an administrative processing timetable.
impact_families.uncertainty: Applicable deadline interpretation could harmonise inclusion of the named day.

impact_families.title: Latvian low-salt condition states the same mass rather than an equivalent amount
impact_families.effect: A food exceeding 0.12 g salt but remaining within the salt amount equivalent to 0.12 g sodium could fail an identical-mass low-salt condition.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading changes the substantive compositional threshold across a range of salt contents, affecting eligibility for the regulated claim.
impact_families.uncertainty: The sodium alternative and equivalence elsewhere support retaining an equivalent-amount test.

impact_families.title: Italian makes adoption of appropriate health-claim guidance discretionary
impact_families.effect: Guidelines are considered appropriate but are not adopted under the Italian discretionary wording.
impact_families.rationale: The changed duty concerns implementation guidance. Authorisation, eligibility and the underlying information requirements remain operative without those guidelines.
impact_families.uncertainty: The broad appropriateness qualification may reduce the practical distinction.

impact_families.title: Estonian data protection condition requires exclusive use rights
impact_families.effect: An applicant with exclusive regulatory reference rights but shared other-use rights fails the Estonian exclusivity condition despite satisfying the remaining protection conditions.
impact_families.rationale: The distinction can determine eligibility for Article 21’s five-year protection against use of application data for a subsequent applicant’s benefit.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 21(2) supports interpreting use as regulatory reliance.

impact_families.title: Maltese reduced-saturated-fat calculation permits an alternative fatty-acid total
impact_families.effect: A product reducing saturated fat by 30% while leaving trans fat unchanged could pass the Maltese single-category calculation despite falling short of a 30% combined reduction.
impact_families.rationale: The alternative calculation can remove the substantive combined-fat reduction required for eligibility, even while the other reduction and no-increase conditions are met.
impact_families.uncertainty: The combined comparator and surrounding provisions support a harmonising combined-total reading.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian immediate-sale exemption refers to unpackaged food
impact_families.effect: Food prepacked for immediate sale and bearing relevant claims could require nutrition labelling and diet and consumption information despite the English exemption.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading removes an entire expressly identified category from an exemption to mandatory labelling and health-claim conditions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation could restore the prepacked category; other applicable exemptions must still be considered.

impact_families.title: Latvian makes the Commission's opinion conditional instead of consultation
impact_families.effect: Without a Member State request or a finding of usefulness, the Commission could have to consult the Committee without being required to issue an opinion.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes consultation and opinion duties; it does not remove the six-month standstill or the consequences of a negative opinion.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may restore the condition's allocation; no further substantive consequence is established.

impact_families.title: Czech authorisation particulars make warning channels alternatives
impact_families.effect: An authorisation requires a protective claim-specific warning on the label alone, allowing advertising carrying the claim to omit it.
impact_families.rationale: The alternative can narrow a protective authorisation condition. Article 10(2) does not independently require the advertising warning where the food has labelling.
impact_families.uncertainty: The final authorisation may require both channels; no actual omission or resulting harm is established.

impact_families.title: Italian generic-descriptor rules emphasise speed instead of transparency
impact_families.effect: Published application rules ensure prompt handling but provide no transparency about individual processing.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns an ancillary procedural objective. Publication remains mandatory, and the provision does not specify a changed substantive derogation entitlement.
impact_families.uncertainty: Publication and applicable procedural principles may substantially harmonise the practical obligations.

impact_families.title: French allows alternative health-information channels without labelling
impact_families.effect: An applicable excessive-consumption warning is supplied in presentation but omitted from advertising carrying a health claim for an unlabelled food.
impact_families.rationale: The alternative reading materially narrows the health-warning duty imposed as a condition of claim use. Article 1(2) does not exempt that warning.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may require disclosure in each channel carrying the claim.

impact_families.title: Croatian appetite-claim categories describe body-weight changes
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualifying appetite claim without a weight-change effect cannot use Article 13(1)(c)’s listed-claims route under the Croatian reading.
impact_families.rationale: The category determines access to a route allowing claim use without the individual procedures in Articles 15 to 19.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 13(1)(a) or contextual interpretation may preserve the route for some appetite claims.

impact_families.title: Latvian energy-free limit excludes equality
impact_families.effect: A product exactly at the ordinary energy-free ceiling could qualify in English but fail the Latvian condition.
impact_families.rationale: The established difference concerns equality at one nutrition designation's threshold, without changing the general permission to sell the food.
impact_families.uncertainty: Measurement and rounding rules are not supplied.

impact_families.title: Czech five-month opinion deadline is an endeavour obligation
impact_families.effect: The Authority exceeds the applicable five-month period despite adequate efforts, without breaching the Czech endeavour obligation.
impact_families.rationale: The established change concerns procedural timing. The Regulation supplies no automatic authorisation, refusal, compensation or other major consequence when this period expires.
impact_families.uncertainty: The extension mechanism may support interpreting the Czech period as binding.

impact_families.title: Latvian disease-risk warning presents multiple factors as a possibility
impact_families.effect: An operator could use a warning saying that multiple risk factors are possible rather than affirming that they exist.
impact_families.rationale: The change narrows supplementary warning content while retaining the uncertain-benefit statement and the special authorisation requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation could require an affirmative multiple-factor statement.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian low-energy limits exclude equality
impact_families.effect: A food exactly at its applicable low-energy ceiling could satisfy the English condition but fail the Lithuanian condition.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence is confined to equality at this nutrition-claim boundary; the thresholds otherwise govern the same range and do not prohibit sale of the food.
impact_families.uncertainty: Measurement and rounding rules are not supplied.

impact_families.title: Greek proprietary-data justification omits express verifiability
impact_families.effect: An application initially proceeds with a relevant explanation for proprietary treatment that lacks checkable support.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns dossier supporting material. It does not itself remove Article 21's designation, exclusive-reference and necessity conditions for protection.
impact_families.uncertainty: Implementing rules or administrative interpretation may require equivalent verification.

impact_families.title: Latvian monitoring notification requests a claim specimen instead of a label
impact_families.effect: An operator could satisfy a market-notification requirement with a specimen claim instead of a model of the product label.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows an ancillary monitoring document; substantive requirements and the separate power to request compliance evidence remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Authorities could request the specimen in its label context or seek further compliance evidence.

impact_families.title: Czech evaluation mandate names overweight
impact_families.effect: The Commission evaluates overweight generally without separately addressing obesity and treats the Czech reporting mandate as satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects an institutional report's subject matter without directly altering claim eligibility, marketing permission or individual entitlements.
impact_families.uncertainty: An assessment of overweight and non-communicable diseases could cover obesity.

impact_families.title: Latvian low-fat condition excludes the solid-food boundary
impact_families.effect: A solid food containing exactly 3 g fat per 100 g could lose eligibility for a low-fat claim.
impact_families.rationale: The established effect is confined to equality at a particular claim boundary, without changing the general permission to sell the food.
impact_families.uncertainty: Liquid-limit syntax and measurement or rounding treatment remain unresolved.

impact_families.title: Croatian no-added-salt condition may exclude naturally occurring sodium in ingredients
impact_families.effect: A product with no added salt and sodium below the ceiling loses eligibility because an ingredient contains naturally occurring sodium.
impact_families.rationale: The changed ingredient condition directly removes permission to use an expressly regulated nutrition claim under Article 8 and the Annex.
impact_families.uncertainty: The no-added-salt heading supports restricting the ingredient condition to added sodium or salt.

impact_families.title: Latvian low-energy limits exclude equality
impact_families.effect: A food exactly at its applicable low-energy ceiling could qualify under English but fail the Latvian numerical condition.
impact_families.rationale: The difference is limited to equality at the claim thresholds, with no supported wider change to food-marketing permission.
impact_families.uncertainty: Measurement and rounding treatment are not supplied.

impact_families.title: Latvian nutrient-profile derogation ties the warning to reduction information
impact_families.effect: A non-reduction nutrition claim could lose the single-nutrient derogation because there is no reduction statement against which to place its warning.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition could exclude a class of nutrition claims from an express exception to nutrient-profile compliance.
impact_families.uncertainty: The reduction reference could be interpreted contextually as referring to the nutrition claim generally.

impact_families.title: Czech disease-risk definition omits the risk-factor endpoint
impact_families.effect: A claim asserting significant reduction of a disease risk factor, without asserting reduced disease-development risk, falls outside the Czech Article 14 category.
impact_families.rationale: The definition governs eligibility for a special authorisation category and its associated conditions, materially changing the regulatory treatment of disease-related claims.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 14(2)'s express risk-factor statement strongly supports a harmonised interpretation.

impact_families.title: Greek endorsement provision refers broadly to health-related institutions
impact_families.effect: A non-charitable health institution is treated as falling within Article 11's national-rules provision.
impact_families.rationale: The broader scope is plausible, but the national rules and overlap with Article 12(c)'s association category are absent. A changed permission cannot be established.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Greek term may denote charitable foundations in context.

impact_families.title: Italian weight-loss prohibition specifies percentage rather than rate
impact_families.effect: A claim referring to rapid weight loss without specifying a percentage or amount escapes this particular prohibition under the Italian reading.
impact_families.rationale: The difference can narrow an outright prohibition. The remaining authorisation and substantiation requirements do not necessarily prohibit every reference to speed.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation may include temporal rate within the Italian restriction.

impact_families.title: Romanian may condition the profile derogation on the claim’s wording
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualifying reduction claim that mentions the relevant nutrient profile could require rewording to obtain the Romanian derogation.
impact_families.rationale: The express derogation preserves the substantive exemption. The supported additional restriction concerns the claim’s reference to a profile, which could be removed without changing the product.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context strongly supports treating the Romanian wording as an exemption from profile assessment rather than a wording restriction.

impact_families.title: Greek nutrient statement specifies matching bold type
impact_families.effect: An equally prominent nutrient statement uses different typography and must be redesigned to satisfy the Greek condition.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns presentation of an already-required statement. Nutrient limits, the single-nutrient derogation, proximity and same-side requirements remain unchanged.
impact_families.uncertainty: Matching bold type may be interpreted functionally as equal prominence.

impact_families.title: Dutch nutrient warning requires equal legibility rather than prominence
impact_families.effect: A warning that is equally readable but less visually prominent could satisfy the Dutch display condition.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns relative presentation; warning content, proximity, same-side placement and substantive conditions for the derogation remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Equal legibility could be interpreted in context to require comparable prominence.

impact_families.title: Finnish allows alternative health-information channels without labelling
impact_families.effect: An unlabelled food’s applicable excessive-consumption warning appears in its presentation but is omitted from advertising carrying the health claim.
impact_families.rationale: Article 10(2)(d) makes the warning a condition of claim use. Article 1(2)’s exemptions do not remove that warning requirement.
impact_families.uncertainty: A contextual reading may require disclosure in every channel carrying the claim.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian comparative-claim rule omits an express difference-disclosure duty
impact_families.effect: A comparative nutrition claim could omit the quantitative difference while comparing equal quantities and satisfying the applicable compositional thresholds.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns comparative disclosure. Article 9's comparator restrictions, Annex thresholds and the prohibition of misleading claims remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Other applicable information requirements could require disclosure for a particular claim.

impact_families.title: Finnish disease-risk definition omits reduction of a risk factor
impact_families.effect: A claim asserting reduced disease-development risk qualifies for consideration under Article 14 without asserting reduction of a disease risk factor.
impact_families.rationale: The definition determines eligibility for a special authorisation route and its express derogation, potentially changing permission to make disease-related claims.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 14(2)’s multiple-risk-factor statement supports harmonising the definition; authorisation remains necessary.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian disease-risk definition omits the risk-factor criterion
impact_families.effect: A claim expressly addressing a disease risk factor could fall outside the Lithuanian Article 14 category, changing its authorisation route and accompanying information requirements.
impact_families.rationale: The definition determines the scope of a core health-claim authorisation category. Exclusion does not itself make the claim lawful under Article 10.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 14(2)'s express risk-factor language strongly supports harmonisation.

impact_families.title: Dutch register category refers to submitted health claims
impact_families.effect: The Commission could have to include submitted but undecided claims in this public register category.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns register coverage. Separate authorisation and list-inclusion requirements continue to govern lawful use of health claims.
impact_families.uncertainty: The cross-references and rejected-claims category strongly favour limiting this category to authorised claims.

impact_families.title: Dutch five-month opinion period is expressed as an endeavour
impact_families.effect: The Authority could miss the applicable deadline despite adequate efforts without breaching the Dutch timing obligation.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns procedural timeliness; the provisions do not make expiry grant authorisation, end assessment or determine substantive eligibility.
impact_families.uncertainty: The express extension mechanism supports interpreting the period as binding.

impact_families.title: Estonian evaluation duty covers overweight
impact_families.effect: The evaluation must address potential effects on overweight beyond the obesity category.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence expands an evaluation report. Article 27 does not itself alter authorisation conditions, remedies or sanctions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The undefined terms may receive an overlapping public-health interpretation.

impact_families.title: Estonian Article 17 makes a protection request trigger restricted-use proceedings
impact_families.effect: A protection request requires the restricted-use route; an otherwise granted authorisation consequently carries a five-year expiry where an ordinary authorisation could have been considered.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed trigger can change the duration of permission. A later unrestricted authorisation requires a further decision under point (b).
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may preserve discretion; neither authorisation nor protection follows automatically from the request.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian opinion-report requirement omits identification of supporting information
impact_families.effect: The Authority could transmit an assessment and reasons without separately identifying the information underlying its opinion.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns report completeness; scientific assessment, reasons, transmission and public availability remain required.
impact_families.uncertainty: Adequate reasons may themselves require identification of the supporting information.

impact_families.title: Spanish five-month opinion deadline is an endeavour obligation
impact_families.effect: Without an applicable extension, the Authority exceeds five months despite adequate efforts and satisfies the Spanish endeavour obligation.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns procedural timing. The supplied text establishes no automatic decision, compensation or other major consequence from expiry.
impact_families.uncertainty: The extension provision and procedural context may support a binding Spanish deadline.

impact_families.title: Croatian Article 17 makes a protection request trigger restricted-use proceedings
impact_families.effect: A protection request requires the restricted-use route, giving an otherwise granted authorisation a five-year expiry where the ordinary route could have remained available.
impact_families.rationale: The supported major consequence is the possible change in authorisation duration. Neither the proposal nor the request itself grants exclusive protection.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 18(5)’s conditional proposal and Article 21 support harmonisation; unrestricted continuation requires another decision.

impact_families.title: Portuguese does not expressly limit the warning derogation to one nutrient
impact_families.effect: When relevant profiles apply, a food exceeding them for several nutrients could obtain the warning-based derogation under the broader Portuguese reading.
impact_families.rationale: That reading expands an exception to the substantive nutrient-profile restriction governing whether nutrition claims may be used.
impact_families.uncertainty: Singular wording and the derogation’s context may establish the same one-nutrient limit; applicable profiles are not supplied.

impact_families.title: Latvian favourable-opinion procedure can constrain the Commission's decision
impact_families.effect: After a favourable scientific opinion, the Commission could be required to conform to it instead of refusing inclusion on another legitimate ground consistent with the Regulation.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading changes decision-making discretion over permission to use a health claim.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 17 and the broader authorisation framework support preserving consideration of other legitimate grounds.

impact_families.title: Czech transitional branches refer to claims subject to national assessment
impact_families.effect: A previously used claim awaiting assessment enters the national notification branch instead of the branch requiring an application before 19 January 2008.
impact_families.rationale: The branches impose different gateways to continued transitional use. Reclassification can determine whether that substantive permission remains available.
impact_families.uncertainty: The required national evaluation report supports limiting the notification branch to claims already assessed.

legislation.title: DIRECTIVE 2009/24/EC OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 23 April 2009 on the legal protection of computer programs (Codified version) (Text with EEA relevance)

unavailable_languages.name: Irish
unavailable_languages.reason: No official language expression exists for this exact version in Cellar metadata.

passages.label: Title
passages.text:
DIRECTIVE 2009/24/EC OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL
of 23 April 2009
on the legal protection of computer programs
(Codified version)
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND THE COUNCIL OF THE EUROPEAN UNION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty establishing the European Community and in particular Article 95 thereof,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to the proposal from the Commission,

passages.label: Citation 3
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee ( 1 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 4
passages.text: Acting in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 251 of the Treaty ( 2 ) ,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | The content of Council Directive 91/250/EEC of 14 May 1991 on the legal protection of computer programs ( 3 ) has been amended ( 4 ) . In the interests of clarity and rationality the said Directive should be codified.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | The development of computer programs requires the investment of considerable human, technical and financial resources while computer programs can be copied at a fraction of the cost needed to develop them independently.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | Computer programs are playing an increasingly important role in a broad range of industries and computer program technology can accordingly be considered as being of fundamental importance for the Community's industrial development.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | Certain differences in the legal protection of computer programs offered by the laws of the Member States have direct and negative effects on the functioning of the internal market as regards computer programs.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | Existing differences having such effects need to be removed and new ones prevented from arising, while differences not adversely affecting the functioning of the internal market to a substantial degree need not be removed or prevented from arising.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | The Community's legal framework on the protection of computer programs can accordingly in the first instance be limited to establishing that Member States should accord protection to computer programs under copyright law as literary works and, further, to establishing who and what should be protected, the exclusive rights on which protected persons should be able to rely in order to authorise or prohibit certain acts and for how long the protection should apply.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | For the purpose of this Directive, the term ‘computer program’ shall include programs in any form, including those which are incorporated into hardware. This term also includes preparatory design work leading to the development of a computer program provided that the nature of the preparatory work is such that a computer program can result from it at a later stage.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | In respect of the criteria to be applied in determining whether or not a computer program is an original work, no tests as to the qualitative or aesthetic merits of the program should be applied.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | The Community is fully committed to the promotion of international standardisation.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) | The function of a computer program is to communicate and work together with other components of a computer system and with users and, for this purpose, a logical and, where appropriate, physical interconnection and interaction is required to permit all elements of software and hardware to work with other software and hardware and with users in all the ways in which they are intended to function. The parts of the program which provide for such interconnection and interaction between elements of software and hardware are generally known as ‘interfaces’. This functional interconnection and interaction is generally known as ‘interoperability’; such interoperability can be defined as the ability to exchange information and mutually to use the information which has been exchanged.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) | For the avoidance of doubt, it has to be made clear that only the expression of a computer program is protected and that ideas and principles which underlie any element of a program, including those which underlie its interfaces, are not protected by copyright under this Directive. In accordance with this principle of copyright, to the extent that logic, algorithms and programming languages comprise ideas and principles, those ideas and principles are not protected under this Directive. In accordance with the legislation and case-law of the Member States and the international copyright conventions, the expression of those ideas and principles is to be protected by copyright.

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) | For the purposes of this Directive, the term ‘rental’ means the making available for use, for a limited period of time and for profit-making purposes, of a computer program or a copy thereof. This term does not include public lending, which, accordingly, remains outside the scope of this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 13
passages.text: (13) | The exclusive rights of the author to prevent the unauthorised reproduction of his work should be subject to a limited exception in the case of a computer program to allow the reproduction technically necessary for the use of that program by the lawful acquirer. This means that the acts of loading and running necessary for the use of a copy of a program which has been lawfully acquired, and the act of correction of its errors, may not be prohibited by contract. In the absence of specific contractual provisions, including when a copy of the program has been sold, any other act necessary for the use of the copy of a program may be performed in accordance with its intended purpose by a lawful acquirer of that copy.

passages.label: Recital 14
passages.text: (14) | A person having a right to use a computer program should not be prevented from performing acts necessary to observe, study or test the functioning of the program, provided that those acts do not infringe the copyright in the program.

passages.label: Recital 15
passages.text: (15) | The unauthorised reproduction, translation, adaptation or transformation of the form of the code in which a copy of a computer program has been made available constitutes an infringement of the exclusive rights of the author. Nevertheless, circumstances may exist when such a reproduction of the code and translation of its form are indispensable to obtain the necessary information to achieve the interoperability of an independently created program with other programs. It has therefore to be considered that, in these limited circumstances only, performance of the acts of reproduction and translation by or on behalf of a person having a right to use a copy of the program is legitimate and compatible with fair practice and must therefore be deemed not to require the authorisation of the rightholder. An objective of this exception is to make it possible to connect all components of a computer system, including those of different manufacturers, so that they can work together. Such an exception to the author's exclusive rights may not be used in a way which prejudices the legitimate interests of the rightholder or which conflicts with a normal exploitation of the program.

passages.label: Recital 16
passages.text: (16) | Protection of computer programs under copyright laws should be without prejudice to the application, in appropriate cases, of other forms of protection. However, any contractual provisions contrary to the provisions of this Directive laid down in respect of decompilation or to the exceptions provided for by this Directive with regard to the making of a back-up copy or to observation, study or testing of the functioning of a program should be null and void.

passages.label: Recital 17
passages.text: (17) | The provisions of this Directive are without prejudice to the application of the competition rules under Articles 81 and 82 of the Treaty if a dominant supplier refuses to make information available which is necessary for interoperability as defined in this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 18
passages.text: (18) | The provisions of this Directive should be without prejudice to specific requirements of Community law already enacted in respect of the publication of interfaces in the telecommunications sector or Council Decisions relating to standardisation in the field of information technology and telecommunication.

passages.label: Recital 19
passages.text: (19) | This Directive does not affect derogations provided for under national legislation in accordance with the Berne Convention on points not covered by this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 20
passages.text: (20) | This Directive should be without prejudice to the obligations of the Member States relating to the time-limits for transposition into national law of the Directives set out in Annex I, Part B,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: HAVE ADOPTED THIS DIRECTIVE:

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
Object of protection
1. In accordance with the provisions of this Directive, Member States shall protect computer programs, by copyright, as literary works within the meaning of the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works. For the purposes of this Directive, the term ‘computer programs’ shall include their preparatory design material.
2. Protection in accordance with this Directive shall apply to the expression in any form of a computer program. Ideas and principles which underlie any element of a computer program, including those which underlie its interfaces, are not protected by copyright under this Directive.
3. A computer program shall be protected if it is original in the sense that it is the author's own intellectual creation. No other criteria shall be applied to determine its eligibility for protection.
4. The provisions of this Directive shall apply also to programs created before 1 January 1993, without prejudice to any acts concluded and rights acquired before that date.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
Authorship of computer programs
1. The author of a computer program shall be the natural person or group of natural persons who has created the program or, where the legislation of the Member State permits, the legal person designated as the rightholder by that legislation.
Where collective works are recognised by the legislation of a Member State, the person considered by the legislation of the Member State to have created the work shall be deemed to be its author.
2. In respect of a computer program created by a group of natural persons jointly, the exclusive rights shall be owned jointly.
3. Where a computer program is created by an employee in the execution of his duties or following the instructions given by his employer, the employer exclusively shall be entitled to exercise all economic rights in the program so created, unless otherwise provided by contract.

passages.label: Article 3
passages.text:
Article 3
Beneficiaries of protection
Protection shall be granted to all natural or legal persons eligible under national copyright legislation as applied to literary works.

passages.label: Article 4
passages.text:
Article 4
Restricted acts
1. Subject to the provisions of Articles 5 and 6, the exclusive rights of the rightholder within the meaning of Article 2 shall include the right to do or to authorise:
(a) | the permanent or temporary reproduction of a computer program by any means and in any form, in part or in whole; in so far as loading, displaying, running, transmission or storage of the computer program necessitate such reproduction, such acts shall be subject to authorisation by the rightholder;
(b) | the translation, adaptation, arrangement and any other alteration of a computer program and the reproduction of the results thereof, without prejudice to the rights of the person who alters the program;
(c) | any form of distribution to the public, including the rental, of the original computer program or of copies thereof.
2. The first sale in the Community of a copy of a program by the rightholder or with his consent shall exhaust the distribution right within the Community of that copy, with the exception of the right to control further rental of the program or a copy thereof.

passages.label: Article 5
passages.text:
Article 5
Exceptions to the restricted acts
1. In the absence of specific contractual provisions, the acts referred to in points (a) and (b) of Article 4(1) shall not require authorisation by the rightholder where they are necessary for the use of the computer program by the lawful acquirer in accordance with its intended purpose, including for error correction.
2. The making of a back-up copy by a person having a right to use the computer program may not be prevented by contract in so far as it is necessary for that use.
3. The person having a right to use a copy of a computer program shall be entitled, without the authorisation of the rightholder, to observe, study or test the functioning of the program in order to determine the ideas and principles which underlie any element of the program if he does so while performing any of the acts of loading, displaying, running, transmitting or storing the program which he is entitled to do.

passages.label: Article 6
passages.text:
Article 6
Decompilation
1. The authorisation of the rightholder shall not be required where reproduction of the code and translation of its form within the meaning of points (a) and (b) of Article 4(1) are indispensable to obtain the information necessary to achieve the interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs, provided that the following conditions are met:
(a) | those acts are performed by the licensee or by another person having a right to use a copy of a program, or on their behalf by a person authorised to do so;
(b) | the information necessary to achieve interoperability has not previously been readily available to the persons referred to in point (a); and
(c) | those acts are confined to the parts of the original program which are necessary in order to achieve interoperability.
2. The provisions of paragraph 1 shall not permit the information obtained through its application:
(a) | to be used for goals other than to achieve the interoperability of the independently created computer program;
(b) | to be given to others, except when necessary for the interoperability of the independently created computer program; or
(c) | to be used for the development, production or marketing of a computer program substantially similar in its expression, or for any other act which infringes copyright.
3. In accordance with the provisions of the Berne Convention for the protection of Literary and Artistic Works, the provisions of this Article may not be interpreted in such a way as to allow its application to be used in a manner which unreasonably prejudices the rightholder's legitimate interests or conflicts with a normal exploitation of the computer program.

passages.label: Article 7
passages.text:
Article 7
Special measures of protection
1. Without prejudice to the provisions of Articles 4, 5 and 6, Member States shall provide, in accordance with their national legislation, appropriate remedies against a person committing any of the following acts:
(a) | any act of putting into circulation a copy of a computer program knowing, or having reason to believe, that it is an infringing copy;
(b) | the possession, for commercial purposes, of a copy of a computer program knowing, or having reason to believe, that it is an infringing copy;
(c) | any act of putting into circulation, or the possession for commercial purposes of, any means the sole intended purpose of which is to facilitate the unauthorised removal or circumvention of any technical device which may have been applied to protect a computer program.
2. Any infringing copy of a computer program shall be liable to seizure in accordance with the legislation of the Member State concerned.
3. Member States may provide for the seizure of any means referred to in point (c) of paragraph 1.

passages.label: Article 8
passages.text:
Article 8
Continued application of other legal provisions
The provisions of this Directive shall be without prejudice to any other legal provisions such as those concerning patent rights, trade-marks, unfair competition, trade secrets, protection of semi-conductor products or the law of contract.
Any contractual provisions contrary to Article 6 or to the exceptions provided for in Article 5(2) and (3) shall be null and void.

passages.label: Article 9
passages.text:
Article 9
Communication
Member States shall communicate to the Commission the provisions of national law adopted in the field governed by this Directive.

passages.label: Article 10
passages.text:
Article 10
Repeal
Directive 91/250/EEC, as amended by the Directive indicated in Annex I, Part A, is repealed, without prejudice to the obligations of the Member States relating to the time-limits for transposition into national law of the Directives set out in Annex I, Part B.
References to the repealed Directive shall be construed as references to this Directive and shall be read in accordance with the correlation table in Annex II.

passages.label: Article 11
passages.text:
Article 11
Entry into force
This Directive shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .

passages.label: Article 12
passages.text:
Article 12
Addressees
This Directive is addressed to the Member States.

findings.english_quote: The provisions of this Directive shall be without prejudice to any other legal provisions such as those concerning patent rights, trade-marks, unfair competition, trade secrets, protection of semi-conductor products or the law of contract.
findings.title: Potential restriction of the savings clause to listed legal fields
findings.explanation: English Article 8 expressly presents its legal fields as examples within a savings clause covering any other legal provisions. Slovenian preserves provisions concerning the listed fields without expressly making the list illustrative. A restrictive reading could leave an unlisted legal field outside this general savings clause, although Slovenian recital 16 supports a broader interpretation.
